32.0.0.en: After all the faithfulness of Hezekiah and his people to God in cleansing their land of idolatrous worship, sanctifying the Temple and restoring the religious celebrations, the feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread, Hezekiah was surprised by the attack of Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was dominating the world at that time. He attacked the cities of the kingdom of Judah and coveted the fall of Jerusalem and the taking of the whole kingdom of Judah, just as he and the kings before him had seized the northern kingdom of Israel and its capital Samaria only a few days before the days of Hezekiah.

32.0.1.en: We may wonder that God allowed this great affliction to come upon Hezekiah despite his goodness, but if we are patient, we will understand the following:

32.0.2.en: 1- God postponed this affliction until Hezekiah and his people grew strong, were sanctified and worshipped God faithfully; that is, He did not hinder their positive works and their striving toward God.

32.0.3.en: 2- He allowed this attack to test the faith of Hezekiah and his people, and indeed they prayed and sought God with all their hearts.

32.0.4.en: 3- After this God was greatly glorified in crushing the enemies in a way that the people of God had not imagined, so their faith was established.

32.1.0.en: Stopped: blocked up and filled in.

32.1.1.en: When King Hezekiah saw Sennacherib's intention to attack Jerusalem, he took counsel with his leaders, that is, his advisers who lead the people. This shows Hezekiah's concern and his esteem for the opinions of those around him; he was not a despot. After the consultation they agreed on preparations to face Sennacherib; the first was to stop the springs of water around Jerusalem, so that the enemies would find no water to drink and would withdraw from besieging Jerusalem because of their thirst. As for Jerusalem, it had springs of water inside it that supplied it, so it would not suffer thirst if it were besieged, especially since Hezekiah stopped the main spring that supplied Jerusalem and diverted its course from underground into the city (v. 30).

32.2.0.en: A great number of the men of Judah were enthusiastic and hurried to fill in the springs of water surrounding Jerusalem. There was also a small stream beside Jerusalem, which probably filled with rainwater and no longer exists today, and they filled it in as well, so that when the armies of Assyria came to besiege Jerusalem they would find no water and would be forced to withdraw because of their thirst. Here we see the people's concern to defend their country and their reliance on God, so they advanced courageously, not afraid of the forces of Assyria coming against them.

32.2.1.en: The stopping of the waters signifies not handing over our abilities to Satan, so that he may use them to destroy us.

32.3.0.en: To complete the military preparations, Hezekiah rebuilt the broken parts of the wall of Jerusalem and raised it until it reached the towers built on the wall.

32.3.1.en: He also built another wall around Jerusalem to fortify it and to hinder the enemies from reaching it. He also fortified the citadel, which is a part of Jerusalem called the City of David, or the City of Zion, or the Ophel; it is a strong fortress that is difficult to storm, and from it the enemies can be attacked if they try to storm Jerusalem. Hezekiah also prepared many defensive weapons, such as shields, and offensive weapons as well. This shows the faithfulness of Hezekiah and his people, for they did everything in their power to defend Jerusalem, the holy city.

32.3.2.en: These fortifications signify the importance of the spiritual person arming himself with spiritual weapons, which are considered like a wall that protects him from the attacks of the enemy; they are his prayers, his readings, his fasts and all the means of grace.

32.4.0.en: After these preparations Hezekiah did the most important thing, which was to strengthen the faith of his soldiers and encourage them. He gathered the commanders of his armies in the square of Jerusalem and encouraged them that God who is with them is stronger than any enemy, so that they should not be alarmed by the multitude or the strength of Assyria, because God is stronger than the power of men. In this he speaks like Elisha, who encouraged his servant by saying, "they that be with us are more than they that be with them" (2 Kgs 6:16). So the people believed the words of Hezekiah, their faith was established, and they were strengthened and prepared for war.

32.4.1.en: Be confident that God who is with you is stronger than all the powers of the world, so do not be troubled by the changes of the world or the evil of those around you, for God is able to deliver you from their plots. Hold fast to Him in much prayer, do your duties faithfully and be at peace, for He protects you from every evil.

32.5.0.en: Lachish: a fortified city in the kingdom of Judah, located west of Hebron, at a distance of fifteen miles.

32.5.1.en: Sennacherib king of Assyria captured a great city in Judah called Lachish, and then sent his armies to Jerusalem to besiege it and take it. By the hand of his servants Sennacherib sent letters of threat to the people living in Jerusalem and standing on its walls.

32.6.0.en: Sennacherib sent a threat in the form of an exclamation to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, because they were fortifying themselves inside Jerusalem, declaring to them the futility of their trust in the words of Hezekiah their king, who told them that their God would protect them from Assyria. Sennacherib accused Hezekiah of deceiving his people and exposing them to death by hunger and thirst in Jerusalem, which the Assyrians were besieging and would capture.

32.7.0.en: Because of his lack of understanding, Sennacherib told the people that Hezekiah had torn down the altars of his God and had called his people to sacrifice and worship before one altar, which is in the house of the Lord. Of course Sennacherib does not understand the difference between God and the pagan gods, and he thinks that tearing down the altars of the idols is tearing down the altars of God.

32.8.0.en: Sennacherib spoke with arrogance, declaring that he and his fathers had seized all the countries of the world to which they had gone, and that their gods had been unable to protect them from Assyria; therefore the God of the children of Israel would not be able to protect them from the hand of Assyria. The words of Hezekiah, he said, were merely a deception of his people; that is, Sennacherib was affirming the truth of his overwhelming power over all countries, however strong the power of their gods.

32.8.1.en: This shows the ignorance of Sennacherib, because all the pagan gods are demons and have no value before the power of God, the only true God, the God of Israel.

32.8.2.en: Do not be troubled by the logic of weak people around you and their reliance on their own strength, for it is nothing before the power of your God. Fortify yourself in Him, seek His help, walk uprightly before Him, and be sure that He protects you and delivers you.

32.9.0.en: The servants of Sennacherib dared to speak insolently against God and against Hezekiah, more than their king had spoken. And Sennacherib sent letters of threat in which he reviled God and King Hezekiah, affirming his overwhelming power, which would crush Jerusalem.

32.9.1.en: The servants of Sennacherib cried out with loud voices in the Jews' language, which the people of God understand, to frighten them so that they would submit and surrender like the other countries that had surrendered to Assyria, regarding the God of Israel as merely a god like the rest of the gods of the pagan nations.

32.9.2.en: The enemies' insulting of Hezekiah in words, as they spoke against God, is a great honor to Hezekiah, that his name was linked with God, and it confirms his goodness. Therefore do not be troubled if the people of the world insult you because you hold fast to God, His commandments and the teachings of the Church.

32.10.0.en: Hezekiah's prayer and its answer are mentioned in detail in (2 Kgs 19:14-36) and were explained there; here, the writer refers to it briefly, and makes clear how the prayer of King Hezekiah united with Isaiah the prophet and rose up to heaven, so that God might deliver His people from Assyria. This shows who the true friends are, those who appear in time of hardship, for Isaiah was the supporter of Hezekiah in his prayer, and God answered them both and rescued His people, as appears in the following verses.

32.10.1.en: Be careful in choosing your friends, because spiritual and faithful friends are the ones who remain with you in the midst of affliction, so you are at ease in your friendship with them. How sweet it is to befriend the saints before men, for they help you in your relationship with God and come to your aid in time of hardship.

32.11.0.en: God answered the prayer of Hezekiah and Isaiah, and sent His angel, who killed the mighty men of the Assyrian army.

32.11.1.en: The Book of Kings tells us that the number of those killed was one hundred and eighty-five thousand, that is, He destroyed them utterly, so that King Sennacherib fled to his own country and abandoned the siege of Jerusalem. He entered the temple of his god to cry to him for help, and his two sons, who came forth from his own bowels, fell upon him and killed him, and a third son of his, Esarhaddon, took the throne.

32.11.2.en: Thus God's mockery of the power of the enemies appears, for He destroyed the mighty army that had overrun the whole world but was unable to harm the children of God. Rather, God stretched out His hand and killed the distinguished ones in the army of Sennacherib, killing every mighty man of valor, every leader and every captain, so that the remaining soldiers no longer had any value and were unable to continue besieging Jerusalem.

32.11.3.en: Sennacherib felt his weakness, since all his helpers had been killed, so he fled lest the angel kill him. But God allowed him to be killed a shameful death while under the protection of his pagan gods and by the hand of his own sons, to be a lesson before all the nations, so that no enemy would try to attack the people of God, because their God is stronger than all the gods.

32.12.0.en: By destroying the army of Assyria, God saved His people and His holy city Jerusalem, and the fear of the people of God came upon all the nations around it, and consequently they were secure and under the protection of God.

32.13.0.en: The nations around the kingdom of Judah felt the greatness of King Hezekiah and the power of his God, so they tried to appease Hezekiah by presenting precious gifts and treasures, and he became exceedingly great.

32.14.s.en: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

32.14.0.en: The events of Hezekiah's sickness, his healing and his pride were mentioned in detail and explained in (2 Kgs 20:1-19), and were also mentioned in (Isa 38, 39). Here he speaks briefly about Hezekiah's illness, until he was close to death, and then he prayed, and God healed him and gave him a sign, which was the shadow going back ten degrees. When a delegation came from Babylon he became proud and showed them his greatness and his treasures, and did not thank God, who had bestowed on him this miraculous healing, but was occupied with his greatness before men. So God's decision, by the mouth of Isaiah, was that all these treasures would be carried to Babylon, and that some of his sons would be taken as slaves to the king of Babylon, but not in the days of Hezekiah; so the king and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem humbled themselves and repented before God. God's punishment took place in this Babylonian captivity, whose direct cause was the departure of the kings and the people from God in the days of the captivity and their refusal to repent, unlike the righteous Hezekiah, who, when he sinned, humbled himself and repented, and his people were influenced by him, so they humbled themselves and repented as he did.

32.14.1.en: God's love for Hezekiah appears in that He allowed him to be broken and to feel his great weakness before the power of Assyria, and then to be completely broken when death approached him, until he reached death to the world and the emptying of his own will, with no hope except God. So he prayed a deep prayer both times, and here he enjoyed hearing the voice of God, who spoke to him by the mouth of Isaiah; for his experience of hearing God came when he was completely broken. There is no way to enjoy God except by becoming a stranger to the world, rising above its material things and cutting off all desires.

32.15.0.en: Stalls: feeding troughs for the cattle in which they eat, that is, stables.

32.15.1.en: God blessed Hezekiah for his goodness, which was mentioned in (chs. 29-32), and gave him great wealth, so that he made treasuries for silver, gold and precious stones, as well as treasuries for spices and precious vessels, in addition to storehouses for weapons, such as shields. He also made storehouses for grain such as wheat, and storehouses for the wine produced from the many vineyards he owned, and other storehouses for storing oil. God also gave him many cattle, so he made stalls for the oxen, the sheep and all kinds of beasts, and built towers in the midst of these stalls to care for them.

32.15.2.en: But, sadly, abundance of wealth helped Hezekiah toward pride, so God was angry with him, although at the beginning of his reign, when he was poor, his distinguished goodness appeared.

32.15.3.en: God's blessings show His love for those who fear Him, and they come in material forms, but when a person matures spiritually He gives him what is greater, that is, spiritual blessings, so he feels God with him and enjoys His fellowship. Be upright and hold fast to God's commandments, and you will enjoy blessings all your days.

32.16.0.en: Gihon: a main spring that supplies Jerusalem, located in the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem and south of the Temple, and in it, higher than another lower spring in the same place.

32.16.1.en: Among the most important works Hezekiah did was providing water for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, by making a lower channel underground, that is, a tunnel that comes out of the upper spring of Gihon and enters inside Jerusalem. God blessed this work, which made it difficult to besiege Jerusalem and expose its inhabitants to thirst. God also blessed the works of Hezekiah on account of his piety and goodness.

32.16.2.en: This lower channel, in which the water flows underground, signifies the hidden work of the Holy Spirit inside the heart, to water it and satisfy it.

32.17.0.en: Interpreters: plural of interpreter, meaning a messenger who knows more than one language; here it means the messengers of Babylon, who know the Babylonian and the Jewish languages.

32.17.1.en: Hezekiah was exposed to two trials: the attack of the army of the Assyrians, and then the trial of his illness and his facing death. In both trials he took refuge in God, who rescued him from the hand of Assyria by sending the angel who killed the mighty men of the Assyrian army. In the mortal illness He healed him and gave him a clear wonder in the whole land, which was the going back of the shadow ten degrees.

32.17.2.en: But he was exposed to a third trial, which was a test from God, when messengers came to him from Babylon, since they had seen the wonder of the shadow going back, to congratulate him on his healing. Hezekiah fell in the trial and became proud, and showed them his wealth and his treasures and valuables that show his greatness, and did not take refuge in God in prayer before showing them what he had. But he returned and repented, after Isaiah the prophet rebuked him and announced God's punishment for him because of his pride; and when he repented, God made this punishment take place after his lifetime, that is, in the days of his descendants, who departed from God, so the disaster of the Babylonian captivity came upon them.

32.17.3.en: We notice that the Book of Chronicles here focuses on Hezekiah's goodness and his great works and not his sins, because it presents the righteous kings of Judah as types of Christ.

32.18.0.en: His goodness: his good deeds and righteous works.

32.18.1.en: The details of the life of King Hezekiah and his righteous works are not written in the Holy Bible, but are mentioned in a book called the Vision of Isaiah the prophet, which is among a collection of books called the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel, and these are historical books and not part of the Holy Bible.

32.19.0.en: The chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David: the best and greatest place among these tombs.

32.19.1.en: After that Hezekiah died, and they buried him in the greatest place among the tombs of the City of David. The people of Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah mourned for him and made many honors for him, perhaps lamentation, dirges and a great burning, as they were accustomed in ancient times, and then his son Manasseh reigned in his place.

32.19.2.en: Note: See the life of Hezekiah at the end of the book.

32.19.3.en: Manasseh and Amon, kings of Judah
